questions.scenario: A `@Transactional` method saves a statement header and then calls `Files.readAllLines(file)`, which throws `IOException`. The header row stays in the database.
questions.question: Why, and what is the fix?
options: By default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions; add rollbackFor = Exception.class (or IOException.class)
readOnly must be set to true
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions commit by default; declare rollback rules explicitly when they must undo work.

questions.scenario: An audit insert is marked `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)` and called from `transfer()` in the same class. When the transfer fails, the audit row disappears too.
questions.question: Why?
options: The call goes through `this`, bypassing the proxy, so the audit runs in the transfer's transaction; move it to a separate bean
questions.explanation: Self-invocation never reaches the proxy that would start the new transaction.

questions.scenario: An outer `@Transactional` method calls `feeService.apply()` (also `@Transactional`, default propagation), catches its RuntimeException and continues. On commit Spring throws `UnexpectedRollbackException`.
questions.question: What happened?
options: The inner method joined the same transaction and marked it rollback-only when it threw; catching the exception didn't undo that
Propagation REQUIRED always throws on commit
questions.explanation: With REQUIRED both methods share one transaction; an inner failure marks it rollback-only.

questions.scenario: A singleton service has a prototype-scoped `ReportBuilder` injected through its constructor, expecting a fresh builder per request. Reports start mixing data.
questions.question: What is wrong?
options: Constructor injection is not allowed for prototypes
The prototype was injected once when the singleton was created; use ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder>.getObject() each time
questions.explanation: Injection happens once; ask the container for a new prototype instance when you need one.

questions.scenario: A nightly `@Scheduled` interest job is deployed on two pods behind a load balancer. Customers receive interest twice.
questions.question: What is the best fix?
options: Ensure only one instance runs it (ShedLock or a database advisory lock, or a platform scheduler) and make the job idempotent
questions.explanation: Every instance runs every @Scheduled method; distributed locking plus idempotency prevents double posting.

questions.scenario: A transfer service sends a confirmation SMS from an `@EventListener`. Some customers get SMSs for transfers that later rolled back.
questions.question: What should change?
options: Use @TransactionalEventListener (AFTER_COMMIT) so the listener runs only after a successful commit
questions.explanation: Plain @EventListener runs synchronously inside the publisher's transaction.

questions.scenario: Which statements about Spring proxies are true? (Choose two.)
questions.question: Select two.
options: Self-invocation always goes through the proxy
Proxies are created before the constructor runs
Annotations like @Transactional and @Cacheable don't apply to private methods
Objects created with `new` don't get Spring's proxy-based behaviour
questions.explanation: Proxies wrap Spring-managed beans after initialisation and only intercept external calls to proxyable methods.

questions.scenario: A service is missing a `DataSource` at start-up after an upgrade, and the team can't tell why auto-configuration skipped it.
questions.question: What is the quickest way to find out?
options: Start with --debug (or the Actuator conditions endpoint) and read the conditions evaluation report
questions.explanation: The report lists which auto-configurations matched or didn't, and the condition responsible.
